issues.legal_issue: Disputes between a landlord and tenant under the general law governing leases are arbitrable when no special statutory regime reserves them to an exclusive court.
material_facts: The dispute concerned a lease of premises and the tenant’s failure to deliver possession after the lease expired.
The lease contained an arbitration clause covering disputes arising from the agreement or its subject matter.
The dispute was governed by the Transfer of Property Act, and no special rent statute conferred exclusive jurisdiction on a specified court.
The applicable law provided limited relief against forfeiture, but the Court found that this did not exclude arbitration.
issues.conclusion: Disputes about determination of a lease under the Transfer of Property Act, including grounds considered alongside the statutory reliefs against forfeiture, are arbitrable. The Court considered the contrary reasoning in Himangni Enterprises to require reconsideration by a larger Bench.
issues.legal_principle: Under Booz Allen and Hamilton Inc. v. SBI Home Finance Ltd., civil and commercial disputes are in principle arbitrable unless legislation expressly or by necessary implication reserves them to public fora. The non-arbitrability example in Booz Allen concerns tenancy matters governed by special statutes that protect tenants against eviction and confer jurisdiction on specified courts; Natraj Studios (P) Ltd. v. Navrang Studios involved such an exclusive statutory forum. Sections 111, 114 and 114A of the Transfer of Property Act identify grounds for lease determination and limited relief against forfeiture, but do not make those disputes triable only by a civil court. The Act is silent on arbitrability and does not negate it. The Court also relied on Olympus Superstructures Pvt. Ltd. v. Meena Vijay Khetan in rejecting the proposition that statutory discretion alone bars arbitration.

rule.if: landlord_tenant_dispute and ordinary_property_lease and arbitration_agreement_exists and no_exclusive_tenant_forum

predicates.landlord_tenant_dispute: A dispute arose between a landlord and a tenant concerning their lease relationship.
predicates.ordinary_property_lease: The lease and dispute were governed by general property law rather than a special tenancy regime.
predicates.arbitration_agreement_exists: The parties agreed to refer disputes arising from their agreement or its subject matter to arbitration.
predicates.no_exclusive_tenant_forum: No applicable special law both protected the tenant against eviction and reserved the dispute to a specified court.

issues.definition: When a landlord-tenant dispute concerns an ordinary property-law lease, the parties agreed to arbitration, and no special law reserves the dispute to an exclusive court, the lease dispute is arbitrable.

issues.legal_issue: A stay of substantially progressed arbitral proceedings may be lifted while an appeal concerning the appointment of an arbitrator is disposed of, with execution of the resulting award made subject to the Court’s permission.
material_facts: The appeal concerned an order appointing an arbitrator.
The arbitral proceedings had begun and 18 sittings had taken place.
The Court had previously stayed the arbitral proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The Court lifted the stay and allowed the arbitration to continue to an award, which could not be executed without applying to the Court.
issues.legal_principle: In light of the circumstances of the case, particularly the substantial progress of the arbitration, the Court exercised its discretion to permit the proceedings to continue while restricting execution of any award pending an application to the Court. No earlier case was cited for this case-specific procedural direction.

predicates.appeal_concerns_arbitrator_appointment: An appeal challenged a decision appointing an arbitrator.
predicates.arbitration_is_ongoing: The arbitral proceedings had started and had not concluded.
predicates.arbitration_has_substantially_progressed: A substantial number of arbitral hearings had already taken place.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an arbitrator’s appointment and the arbitration is ongoing and substantially progressed, the arbitration may continue, but execution of its award requires court permission.
